meta.name: Brittany First Year Costs
meta.excerpt: Brittany first-year costs run $2,800–$6,000 including purchase price. Exercise infrastructure and hunting gear (for field dogs) are the variable costs. Grooming is genuinely inexpensive for this breed.

intro.label: Upfront Costs
intro.heading: What Does It Cost to Bring Home a Brittany?
intro.html:
Brittanys are bred along two distinct lines — field and show — and the price tag tracks that split closely. A puppy from a reputable breeder runs $800–$2,500. Field-bred Brittanys out of proven hunting stock tend to land at $1,200–$2,500, since buyers are paying for working drive and pedigree performance, not just conformation. Show-line puppies from health-tested parents are usually $1,000–$2,000. The American Brittany Club keeps a breeder directory, and it's worth using it — ask specifically for OFA hip and elbow clearances plus eye certifications on both parents. Hip dysplasia is a documented issue in this breed, and a breeder who can't produce clearance paperwork is a red flag regardless of how nice the litter looks in photos.

Rescue and Adoption Route

Rescue adoption runs $150–$400 through breed-specific Brittany rescues or general sporting-dog rescue networks. A striking number of rescue Brittanys land in foster care simply because their owners underestimated how much daily activity this dog actually needs — not because of behavioral problems the dog created on its own. That means an active household adopting a rescue Brittany is often getting a structurally sound, otherwise easy-to-live-with dog for a fraction of breeder pricing. The tradeoff is less certainty about field drive, hip status, and early socialization history, so ask the rescue for any vet records or x-rays already on file.

Initial Setup: $250–$500

ItemCost
Crate (medium to large, 36–42 inches)$60–$120
Dog bed$50–$100
Collar, harness, leash$50–$100
Grooming tools (slicker brush, comb, blunt-tip scissors)$40–$80
Bowls$25–$50
Fetch toys and enrichment$30–$50

Buy the crate at adult size from day one rather than upgrading twice — a 30–40 lb dog needs the larger crate eventually anyway, and a divider panel handles the puppy phase for a few extra dollars instead of a second purchase.

Exercise Infrastructure: $0–$1,500

This is the line item that varies most by household, and it matters more for a Brittany than for a lower-drive breed. A Brittany bred to cover ground all day in an open field will test a weak fence line and find a gap in a hedge you didn't know existed. If secure fencing isn't already in place, budget for it — a 4–6 foot fence installation for a typical suburban backyard runs anywhere from a few hundred dollars for a partial run to $1,000–$1,500 for full perimeter fencing. This isn't as absolute a requirement as it is for a sighthound with a hard prey drive, but a Brittany without a secure space to burn energy is a Brittany who redirects that energy into your furniture, your doors, and your patience.

Regional Price Variation

Urban buyers on the coasts should expect puppy prices, professional bathing, and fencing installation to run toward the top of every range quoted here — sometimes 15–25% above the national average in metro markets like Seattle, Boston, or the Bay Area. Suburban and rural Midwest and Southern buyers often land closer to the bottom of the range, and field-line breeders are frequently concentrated in rural areas anyway, which can offset travel costs against lower purchase prices.

care.label: First Year Recurring
care.heading: First Year Ongoing Expenses, Month by Month
care.html:
Food: $500–$750 for the first year, or $40–$65 per month. A 30–40 lb adult Brittany eats roughly 1.5–2.5 cups of quality dry kibble per day depending on activity level and formula density — and a field-trained or actively hunting Brittany at the high end of that range, since the breed's energy output demands real caloric support. A 30-lb bag of a performance-formula kibble suited to a sporting breed typically lasts 5–7 weeks for one dog, which is where most of that monthly figure comes from. Puppies eat a puppy-specific formula through roughly 12 months, then transition to adult food; budget the switch around the one-year mark rather than rushing it, since large-breed-style growth-rate control isn't a major concern for a 30–40 lb dog the way it is for giant breeds.

Month 1–3: Setup-Heavy

The first three months front-load cost. This is when the crate, bed, leash, bowls, and grooming tools get purchased, when the puppy vaccine series runs its course, and when spay or neuter is often scheduled. Expect $700–$1,400 in this window alone once you include a chunk of the setup costs and the first two vet visits.

Month 4–6: Vaccines Finish, Training Starts

The vaccine series wraps up, heartworm and flea/tick prevention becomes a monthly recurring line, and this is the ideal window to enroll in a puppy obedience class — a Brittany's willingness to work with people makes this stage genuinely enjoyable rather than a battle. Budget $150–$350 for this stretch between prevention and the first obedience course.

Month 7–12: Steady State Begins

Food and prevention become routine, a field-line puppy may start informal bird introduction or a hunt-test prep class, and any remaining setup costs (extra fencing, a second crate for the car) get finished. This period runs $250–$500 depending on how much structured training is added.

Veterinary Care (First Year): $400–$800

  • Initial wellness exam and puppy vaccination series: $150–$350
  • Spay or neuter: $150–$400
  • Heartworm and parasite prevention: $100–$200/year for a medium breed
  • OFA hip and elbow pre-screening: many breeders complete this before sale — ask for the parents' documentation rather than assuming it exists

Pet Insurance and the Brittany's Health Profile

Pet insurance runs $400–$900/year and is genuinely worth carrying on this breed. Hip dysplasia, epilepsy, and hypothyroidism are the three conditions that show up repeatedly in Brittany health records, and none of them are cheap surprises if they arrive uninsured. Enroll before the first vet visit if possible — a condition noted at any exam can become a pre-existing exclusion the moment it's on paper, and epilepsy in particular is often diagnosed only after a first seizure with no warning signs beforehand.

Grooming: $40–$200/year

The Brittany's medium, flat-to-wavy coat with light feathering on the ears, legs, and underbelly is genuinely one of the easier sporting-dog coats to maintain at home. A weekly brushing session with a slicker brush and comb — the $40–$80 one-time tool investment covers this — keeps the coat mat-free and manages shedding. The feathering needs occasional trimming with blunt-tip scissors to keep debris from field work or brush from tangling in it. Ear cleaning deserves real attention: the Brittany's floppy ears restrict airflow, and a dog that's been swimming, retrieving from water, or working in humid brush is at real risk of ear infections if the ears aren't dried and checked regularly. Some owners add occasional professional bathing after a hard hunting season, at $50–$80 per session, but it's a convenience purchase, not a necessity.

Training: $200–$600

A Brittany's biddable, eager temperament makes basic obedience genuinely easy to teach — puppy class plus a follow-up obedience course runs $200–$400. The real value-add for this breed is structured field or nose work training, which channels the pointing-and-flushing instinct into something productive. Field training or hunting-dog classes for field-line dogs add $200–$600 or more for formal instruction, but for a breed whose whole genetic purpose is bird work, this money buys behavioral stability as much as skill.

Exercise Activities: $50–$300/year

Hunt tests, agility, and other organized dog sports give a Brittany's drive somewhere productive to go. Entry fees, club memberships, and travel to events add up modestly — $50–$300 annually depending on how involved you get — and dogs enrolled in these activities are, anecdotally, far less likely to end up in the rescue pipeline for behavior problems tied to boredom.

special.label: Total & Ongoing
special.heading: First-Year Total, Long-Term Costs, and Ways to Save
special.html:
First-year total estimate: $2,800–$6,000, purchase price included. The spread is driven mostly by three variables: whether you bought a field-line or show-line puppy, whether fencing needed to go in, and how much formal field training was added.

Budget Path vs. Premium Path

Both paths produce a healthy, well-adjusted Brittany. The premium path buys documented health screening, formal field development, and secure fencing up front; the budget path relies more on your own vigilance and a rescue's existing groundwork.

Annual Ongoing Costs After Year One: $1,200–$2,200

  • Food: $500–$750
  • Routine vet care and preventives: $300–$550
  • Pet insurance: $400–$900
  • Grooming: minimal at home, or occasional professional bathing

Health Cost Scenarios Worth Planning For

Hip dysplasia is the structural concern most likely to generate a large one-time bill. Mild cases may need only weight management and joint supplements, but significant cases can require surgery at $2,000–$6,000 per joint — this is exactly why OFA-cleared parentage and insurance enrolled before any lameness shows up both matter so much for this breed specifically. Epilepsy shows up in a meaningful slice of the Brittany population and, once diagnosed, typically means lifelong anticonvulsant medication running $500–$2,000/year, plus periodic bloodwork to monitor liver values on the medication. Hypothyroidism is comparatively easy to manage — daily thyroid medication runs $200–$600/year and, once dosed correctly, rarely causes further complications. None of these three conditions is a guaranteed outcome, but all three are common enough in the breed that a Brittany-specific insurance policy earns its premium more reliably than it would for a breed without this documented profile.

Money-Saving Tactics That Don't Cut Corners

  • Ask the breeder for OFA clearance paperwork up front — a $50 request that can prevent a $2,000–$6,000 surgery bill down the road.
  • Enroll in insurance before the first vet visit, not after — the cost is identical, but the coverage is broader.
  • Use a hunt club or field-training co-op instead of private one-on-one instruction where your dog just needs bird exposure and structure, not remedial correction.
  • Buy fencing material in the off-season if you're installing it yourself; labor and material costs on fencing often dip outside peak spring installation demand.

The false economy to avoid with this breed is skipping exercise infrastructure to save money short-term. A Brittany without a secure yard or a real daily outlet doesn't get cheaper — it gets more expensive, in the form of destroyed furniture, escaped-dog recovery costs, or a dog eventually surrendered to rescue because the household couldn't keep up. The exercise commitment is not optional, and neither, functionally, is a safe space to meet it.

Lifetime Cost

Over a 12–14 year lifespan, total ownership cost excluding purchase price typically runs $14,000–$28,000 depending on health outcomes and activity level. Relative to its size and energy output, the Brittany is not an expensive breed to keep — the real investment this dog asks for is your time and your willingness to move, not your wallet.

faq.q: Is a Brittany expensive to own overall?
faq.a: It's a moderate-cost breed. Purchase price is accessible compared to many sporting breeds, food costs are reasonable for a 30–40 lb dog, and the coat is genuinely cheap to maintain at home. The real cost is time — this breed needs serious daily exercise, and a household that can't provide it will end up paying in destroyed property or behavioral fallout instead of dollars. Financially, the breed's known conditions (hip dysplasia, epilepsy, hypothyroidism) make insurance a smart line item, though none of them are typically catastrophic if caught early.

faq.q: What health costs should I actually plan for?
faq.a: Hip dysplasia is the biggest potential bill — significant cases can mean surgery at $2,000–$6,000 per joint, which is why OFA clearances on the parents matter so much at purchase. Epilepsy, if it develops, usually means lifelong medication in the $500–$2,000/year range plus periodic bloodwork. Hypothyroidism is the mildest of the three, managed with inexpensive daily medication around $200–$600/year. Enrolling insurance before any of these show up on a vet record is the single most effective cost-management move you can make.

faq.q: Do field-line Brittanys cost more to keep than show-line dogs?
faq.a: Field-line puppies often cost more upfront from proven hunting stock, and formal field training adds another $200–$600-plus in instructional fees. Day-to-day costs are similar between lines, though a working field dog racks up more coat and paw-pad wear and may need extra vet checks after a hard hunting season. The payoff is that hunt tests and field work are exactly the kind of high-output exercise this breed needs, so the training spend does double duty as your exercise budget.

faq.q: When should I buy pet insurance for a Brittany puppy?
faq.a: Before the first vet visit, ideally the week the puppy comes home. Insurance underwriting treats anything noted at an exam as a potential pre-existing condition, and epilepsy especially tends to appear with no advance warning — a dog can look perfectly healthy at eight weeks and have a first seizure at eighteen months. Enrolling early costs the same $400–$900/year either way; enrolling late risks having the exact conditions this breed is prone to excluded from coverage.

faq.q: Is fencing really necessary, or can I skip it to save money?
faq.a: For a Brittany, skipping it is a false economy. This breed was built to cover open ground at a run, and a weak fence line or an unfenced yard means either constant leash-only exercise (which rarely meets a 90-minute daily requirement) or a dog that eventually finds the gap. Installation runs $0 if you already have secure fencing, up to $1,000–$1,500 for a full suburban perimeter — money that's cheaper in the long run than vet bills from a road accident or the stress of a repeatedly escaping dog.
